before_text: IoT Smart City Architecture for Traffic Optimization1. Edge LayerThe edge layer processes data close to the location where it is collected. In a smart city traffic system, cameras and sensors can monitor vehicle movement, road occupancy, and traffic flow. A nearby Raspberry Pi or other edge device can perform initial processing, filter unnecessary data, and identify useful traffic measurements.Local processing can reduce the amount of raw video sent to the cloud and may allow the system to respond more quickly to certain events. However, edge devices have limited processing power and memory, so computationally intensive tasks may need to be performed elsewhere.2. Cloud Analytics LayerThe cloud analytics layer receives traffic measurements from edge devices and combines information from multiple locations. MQTT can provide lightweight messaging between connected devices and backend services. A cloud platform can store historical measurements, analyze traffic patterns, and display results on a dashboard.City planners can use the dashboard to identify congested intersections, compare traffic patterns over time, and evaluate possible changes to traffic signals. The system should monitor data quality, device connectivity, and message delivery to reduce the risk of making decisions from incomplete information.3. System IntegrationThe edge and cloud layers work together to support traffic monitoring. Edge devices perform local data processing, while cloud services provide centralized storage and broader analysis. Security measures should protect device identities, communication channels, and access to the dashboard.A well-designed architecture can help city authorities understand traffic conditions and make more informed decisions about transportation infrastructure.

before_text: PostgreSQL vs. MongoDB1. Relational Joins and ACID GuaranteesPostgreSQL is a relational database management system that organizes information into tables with defined relationships. SQL joins combine related records from multiple tables. For example, an online shopping application can join customer and order tables to retrieve the orders associated with a particular customer.PostgreSQL supports transactions and ACID properties: Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, and Durability. These properties help ensure that a transaction is completed reliably. If an operation fails before a transaction commits, its changes can be rolled back. 2. Horizontal Sharding and Document FlexibilityMongoDB stores data as documents, commonly organized into collections. Documents can contain nested objects and arrays, allowing related information to be represented in a flexible structure. This approach can be useful when application records contain different attributes.MongoDB also supports horizontal scaling through sharding. Sharding distributes data across multiple servers according to a selected shard key. A suitable shard key can help distribute workloads, although a poor choice may create uneven data distribution or performance bottlenecks.The choice between PostgreSQL and MongoDB depends on data relationships, consistency requirements, query patterns, and scaling needs. Both systems offer useful capabilities, and the decision should be based on measured application requirements rather than a general assumption that one database is always superior.

doc_title: Web Performance Optimization: SSR vs. CSR
before_text: Web Performance Optimization: SSR vs. CSRIntroductionWeb performance influences how quickly users can see and interact with a website. Server-Side Rendering (SSR) and Client-Side Rendering (CSR) are two approaches used to generate web pages. In SSR, the server generates HTML for a request, while CSR commonly relies on JavaScript running in the browser to construct the page.Performance MeasurementsTime to First Byte (TTFB) measures the time between a browser making a request and receiving the first byte of the response. First Contentful Paint (FCP) measures the time until the browser renders the first piece of content, such as text or an image. Both metrics help developers understand different parts of the page-loading process.SSR can display meaningful HTML before the browser finishes executing all application JavaScript. However, server processing and network latency may increase TTFB if the backend is slow. CSR can provide smooth navigation after the application has loaded, but the initial page may depend on downloading and executing JavaScript.Hydration is the process in which JavaScript connects interactive behaviour to HTML that the server has already generated. It allows buttons, forms, and other interface elements to respond to user actions.

before_text: Algorithmic Bias in Higher EducationIntroductionMachine learning systems are increasingly used to support educational decisions, including automated grading, student performance prediction, and personalized learning. However, these systems can produce unfair results when their training data does not adequately represent the students who will be evaluated. Educational institutions must therefore consider fairness, transparency, and accountability when introducing algorithmic decision-making.Training Data and Proxy VariablesTraining data skew occurs when the examples used to develop a model do not accurately represent the wider student population. For example, if a grading model is trained mainly on essays from students with similar educational backgrounds, it may perform less accurately for students who use different writing styles or language patterns.proxy variables canalso introduces bais. A proxy variable is feature that indirectly represents another characteristic. For example, school location or access to educationa resourcesFairness and MitigationSeveral techniques can help reduce algorithmic bias. These include improving dataset representation, evaluating false-positive and false-negative rates across groups, documenting model limitations, and allowing students to request human review. Regular monitoring is necessary because student populations and educational practices can change over time.Automated grading should support educators rather than replace their professional judgment. Institutions should communicate how predictions are used and ensure that students have appropriate opportunities to challenge incorrect outcomes.

before_text: Architectural Tradeoffs in Enterprise Systems1. IntroductionEnterprise applications require software architectures that support business growth, maintainability, and reliable performance. Two common architectural approaches are monolithic architecture and microservices architecture. A monolithic application combines most of its functionality into a single deployable unit, while a microservices architecture divides the application into smaller, independent services. Each approach has advantages and limitations depending on the project's size, technical requirements, and available resources.2. Microservices ScalabilityOne important advantage of microservices is the ability to scale individual services independently. For example, an online shopping application may experience high demand in its payment and product-search services during a promotional event. With microservices, the development team can allocate additional resources to these services without scaling the entire application. This approach can improve resource utilization and reduce unnecessary infrastructure costs.Microservices also allow different teams to develop, test, and deploy services independently. However, distributed communication introduces challenges such as network latency, service failures, monitoring complexity, and data consistency. According to Fowler and Lewis [1], microservices organize applications as collections of independently deployable services. Therefore, organizations must consider both scalability benefits and operational complexity before adopting this architecture.3. Maintenance OverheadAlthough microservices provide flexibility, they can increase maintenance overhead. Developers must manage service communication, authentication, logging, monitoring, and deployment pipelines. A monolithic system may be easier to develop and deploy when an application is small because fewer infrastructure components are required.The CAP theorem describes three important properties of distributed database systems: Consistency, Availability, and Partition Tolerance. Consistency means that clients receive the latest valid data according to the system's consistency guarantees. Availability means that every request to a functioning node receives a response. Partition tolerance means that the system continues operating despite communication failures between nodes.PostgreSQL, MongoDB, and CassandraDifferent databases provide different mechanisms for managing distributed data. MongoDB supports configurable read and write concerns, allowing applications to choose appropriate consistency and durability guarantees. Cassandra offers tunable consistency levels that allow applications to balance response availability and consistency requirements.Database selection depends on the application's needs. A banking application may prioritize strong consistency for financial transactions, while a large content platform may prioritize availability for certain read operations. Developers must understand the consequences of their consistency settings before deploying a distributed system.

before_text: Understanding the CAP Theorem in Distributed DatabasesIntroductionThe CAP theorem describes three important properties of distributed database systems: Consistency, Availability, and Partition Tolerance. Consistency means that clients receive the latest valid data according to the system's consistency guarantees. Availability means that every request to a functioning node receives a response. Partition tolerance means that the system continues operating despite communication failures between nodes.According to the CAP theorem, when a network partition occurs, a distributed system must make a trade-off between consistency and availability. This does not mean that a database can only support two properties under every circumstance. Instead, the theorem describes the choices that become necessary when communication between nodes is disrupted.PostgreSQL, MongoDB, and CassandraDifferent databases provide different mechanisms for managing distributed data. MongoDB supports configurable read and write concerns, allowing applications to choose appropriate consistency and durability guarantees. Cassandra offers tunable consistency levels that allow applications to balance response availability and consistency requirements.Database selection depends on the application's needs. A banking application may prioritize strong consistency for financial transactions, while a large content platform may prioritize availability for certain read operations. Developers must understand the consequences of their consistency settings before deploying a distributed system.

Lanka BuildTech Engineers (Pvt) Ltd: Employment Status, Working Time, Leave, EPF/ETF and Gratuity1. IntroductionIndustrial law regulates employment relationships, protects workers from unfair treatment and establishes duties for employers. Lanka BuildTech Engineers (Pvt) Ltd faces issues concerning the status of Nadeesha and Faiz, working hours and leave, unpaid retirement-fund contributions, and Ranjith’s claim for gratuity after resignation. The relevant framework includes the Shop and Office Employees (Regulation of Employment and Remuneration) Act No. 19 of 1954, the Employees’ Provident Fund Act No. 15 of 1958, the Employees’ Trust Fund Act No. 46 of 1980, the Payment of Gratuity Act No. 12 of 1983 and the Industrial Disputes Act No. 43 of 1950.2. Employment Status: Nadeesha and Faiz2.1 Legal tests for classificationThe distinction is between a contract of service, which creates an employment relationship, and a contract for services, in which a client obtains work from an independent contractor. The label used by the parties is not conclusive; the actual relationship must be assessed. Four tests are relevant:(i) Control test — how far the organisation determines the worker’s hours, location and method of work.(ii) Integration test — whether the work is part of the organisation’s ordinary business.(iii) Economic reality test — who provides equipment, carries costs and risk, and has the opportunity to make a profit.(iv) Multiple-factor test — all circumstances are weighed together, including control and whether there is an ongoing obligation to offer and accept work.2.2 Nadeesha: contract of serviceNadeesha’s circumstances indicate that she is an employee. She attends the head office at fixed times and works under the Chief Engineer’s direct supervision, showing the company’s control over her work. Lanka BuildTech supplies her software and equipment, so she does not appear to bear the costs and risks of an independent business. Her structural-design work is also closely connected to the company’s main services. Although she was recruited during a temporary increase in orders, a short-term appointment can still be employment. The better conclusion is that Nadeesha works under a contract of service.2.3 Faiz: contract for servicesFaiz, by contrast, supplies his own laptop and licensed software, chooses his hours, invoices a fixed fee for each project and may work for other firms at the same time. These facts suggest that he controls the manner of performance, bears his own operating costs and works as an independent business rather than as part of the company’s staff. The facts also suggest there is no continuing obligation for Lanka BuildTech to offer work or for Faiz to accept it. Taken together, the factors support his classification as an independent contractor.2.4 Legal significanceEmployees may claim statutory protection relating to hours, leave, EPF/ETF, qualifying gratuity and employment remedies. A genuine contractor generally relies on the commercial agreement and may pursue unpaid fees through ordinary civil proceedings. An employer may be vicariously liable for an employee’s tort committed in the course of employment, while a contractor is generally responsible for their own acts. Lanka BuildTech should ensure that Faiz’s actual working arrangements remain consistent with contractor status; if the company begins controlling his hours and methods or integrating him into its workforce, the classification should be reconsidered.3. Working Hours, Overtime and Leave3.1 Application of the SOEAThe supplied answer treats the site supervisors, draughtsmen and clerks as covered by the Shop and Office Employees (Regulation of Employment and Remuneration) Act No. 19 of 1954 (SOEA). Although site supervisors work outdoors, they are employed by an office-based business. Their actual working arrangements and the protective purpose of the legislation should therefore be considered rather than assuming that outdoor work alone excludes them.3.2 Working time and overtimeUnder the legal framework in the supplied material, ordinary hours are limited to eight per day and 45 per week. Work beyond the applicable limit attracts overtime at one and a half times the normal rate. Sunday and public-holiday work must be compensated at the statutory rate or, where legally permitted, by a paid day in lieu. The supervisors and draughtsmen reportedly work more than 45 hours weekly, including Sundays and public holidays, without overtime pay or substitute leave. If proven, this practice breaches the applicable requirements.Each affected worker should calculate the claim using actual hours, normal wages, overtime hours, dates worked and any payments already received. Attendance sheets, site records, rosters, payslips and messages assigning weekend work can help substantiate the figures. Employees can ask the Commissioner of Labour to investigate and pursue arrears. A complaint through a trade union or employee representative may also help demonstrate that the practice affects a group of workers.3.3 Annual and casual leaveSection 6 of the SOEA, as described in the supplied answer, provides 14 days of paid annual leave for an employee who has completed more than one year of service. For employees in their first year, the stated entitlement depends on when they started: 10 days for April–June, seven days for July–September, and four days for October–December. The supplied answer also identifies seven days of casual leave per year, accruing at one day for every two months of service.Annual and casual leave are statutory entitlements, not merely benefits granted at management’s discretion. An employer may reasonably organise the timing of leave, but repeated refusal without a valid reason may breach the law. Clerks should keep copies of leave requests, rejection messages and any explanation given by management. These records can help establish their leave balances and whether refusals were justified.3.4 Ishara’s illnessThe supplied answer states that the SOEA does not create a separate sick-leave entitlement. A short illness may be covered by available casual leave, while a more favourable right could arise under Ishara’s contract or company policy. Her claim should therefore be assessed against unused annual and casual leave and any contractual sick-leave terms. If she was denied leave to which she was entitled, or unfairly penalised for absence, she may seek assistance from the Labour Department and consider a Labour Tribunal remedy where available. The company should review her medical evidence and leave balance before making a decision.4. EPF and ETF Contributions4.1 Employer obligationsThe Employees’ Provident Fund Act No. 15 of 1958 requires contributions to EPF. The supplied answer states that the employer contributes 12% of an employee’s total earnings and the employee contributes 8%, giving a combined 20%. This amount must be remitted to the Central Bank by the end of the month after the month in which wages were paid. Under the Employees’ Trust Fund Act No. 46 of 1980, the employer alone contributes 3% to the ETF Board. These obligations are compulsory and cannot be delayed simply because the business has cash-flow difficulties.4.2 Consequences of defaultLanka BuildTech has deducted employees’ EPF shares for eight months but has not remitted the combined contributions. This is particularly serious because the deductions have already been taken from wages and must be held for their statutory purpose. A promise to pay “in due course” does not meet the legal deadlines. The supplied answer identifies possible surcharges, recovery through a certificate enforced in the Magistrate’s Court as if the sum were a fine, and prosecution of the company and responsible directors or officers. The delay also interrupts retirement savings and may affect employees’ access to fund benefits.The company should reconcile payroll with EPF and ETF statements, identify every unpaid month, calculate the arrears and applicable surcharges, and make payment promptly. The Department of Labour can inspect records and take appropriate recovery or enforcement action. Cash-flow problems or an accounting error do not remove the employer’s statutory responsibility. Employees should retain payslips and obtain fund statements to check which contributions have actually been credited.5. Ranjith’s Gratuity Claim5.1 Eligibility and resignationThe Payment of Gratuity Act No. 12 of 1983 governs Ranjith’s claim. Under the conditions set out in the supplied answer, an employee qualifies after five years of continuous service if the establishment employed at least 15 persons during the preceding 12 months. Lanka BuildTech has about 90 staff and Ranjith has served continuously for 16 years, so both thresholds are satisfied on the stated facts.Management says resignation prevents payment. The supplied answer rejects this view, interpreting termination broadly enough to include resignation, retirement and other ways employment may end. On that interpretation, leaving voluntarily to join another firm does not alone defeat an otherwise valid claim. The answer also refers to section 13 as providing for forfeiture in specified serious-misconduct situations, including fraud, misappropriation, wilful damage to property or negligent loss of goods. No such allegation is made against Ranjith. He should therefore receive gratuity, subject to the statutory conditions and any applicable exception.5.2 Calculation and delayFor a monthly-paid employee, the supplied answer calculates gratuity at half a month’s last-drawn salary for each completed year of service. Ranjith’s 16 years therefore produce an amount equal to eight months of his last-drawn salary. Section 5 is identified as requiring payment within 30 days of termination. The supplied answer lists surcharges of 10% for a delay up to one month, 15% for one to three months, 20% for three to six months, 25% for six to twelve months and 30% for more than one year. The company should calculate the exact sum from his final salary and service record and pay it without further delay.6. Remedies and Recommendations6.1 Remedies for employeesUnder section 31B(1) of the Industrial Disputes Act No. 43 of 1950, the supplied answer identifies Labour Tribunal proceedings as a route for certain disputes involving employment terms, unfair practices and gratuity. It refers to the Tribunal’s “just and equitable” approach and cites United Engineering Workers Union v Devanayagam (1967) 69 NLR 289 (PC) and State Bank of India v Edirisinghe. Employees should confirm the proper procedure and any applicable time limits before filing.The group should continue its complaint with the Department of Labour, which can examine records and address overtime, leave and EPF/ETF defaults. Ranjith may complain to the Commissioner about unpaid gratuity; section 8(1) of the Gratuity Act is identified in the supplied answer as allowing a recovery certificate enforceable through the Magistrate’s Court. Employees should preserve payslips, time records, overtime calculations, leave applications and fund statements. These documents will help establish both liability and the amount claimed.6.2 Recommendations for Lanka BuildTech(i) Pay outstanding overtime, remit all unpaid EPF and ETF contributions with applicable surcharges, and settle Ranjith’s gratuity.(ii) Introduce reliable timekeeping, comply with ordinary-hour limits, pay overtime correctly and document lawful substitute days off.(iii) Keep accurate leave balances, assess requests fairly and record reasons for refusals. Clarify sick-leave policy and honour applicable contractual or statutory rights.(iv) Establish monthly fund-remittance procedures, reconcile payroll and fund statements, and assign clear director-level oversight for deadlines.(v) Keep contractor arrangements genuinely project-based and avoid employee-like control over Faiz if independent-contractor status is intended.7. ConclusionOn the facts supplied, Nadeesha is best treated as an employee and Faiz as an independent contractor. The overtime and leave practices raise compliance concerns under the SOEA. The eight-month EPF/ETF default may lead to surcharges, recovery proceedings and prosecution. Ranjith’s service history and the interpretation of the Gratuity Act in the supplied material support his entitlement despite resignation. Prompt payment, proper records and stronger HR and financial controls are necessary to remedy employees’ losses and restore lawful industrial relations.
